study_identification_part.si4_title: Neuroanatomical heterogeneity and homogeneity in individuals at clinical high risk for psychosis

cm1_research_objectives.reason: The study clearly states both research hypotheses and the purpose of applying heterogeneity analysis (similar to normative modeling principles). The paper explicitly describes: (1) Research questions about whether neuroanatomical heterogeneity differs between CHR-P and HC groups, and between CHR-P individuals who transition to psychosis versus those who do not; (2) The purpose is described as gaining a fuller understanding of the CHR-P neuroanatomy, informing development of precision and predictive models of psychosis, and identifying individuals with shared characteristics. Both criteria are satisfied: research hypotheses are provided (expecting increased heterogeneity in CHR-P shown by higher VR and lower PBSI scores), and the purpose of applying person-based indices is described (precision medicine, disease understanding, subgroup identification).
cm1_research_objectives.supporting_text: The present study aimed to apply both group-level and personalised indices to investigate whether neuroanatomical heterogeneity significantly differed between (i) individuals at CHR-P and healthy controls (HC), and (ii) individuals at CHR-P who subsequently transitioned to psychosis and those who did not. | The rationale for these analyses was four-fold. First, the development of a fuller understanding of neuroanatomy of the CHR-P population is necessary to address growing criticisms of the CHR-P paradigm. Second, such work will inform the development of precision and predictive models of psychosis more broadly. Third, this work would allow us to identify individuals with shared characteristics who may be potentially important for research and clinical intervention. Fourth, we wished to scrutinise the clinical relevance associated with neuroanatomical heterogeneity through several subgroup investigations. | We hypothesised that variance in neuroanatomical measures would significantly differ between the CHR-P and HC groups, with individuals at CHR-P demonstrating significantly increased heterogeneity in neuroanatomical measures. Specifically, we expected to observe significantly higher Variability Ratio (VR) effect sizes and significantly lower Person-Based Similarity Index (PBSI) scores in the CHR-P group.

nm9_model_performance_reference_cohort.reason: This study doesn't build a traditional predictive normative model requiring metrics like explained variance or prediction error. However, it does report quantitative metrics for the Person-Based Similarity Index approach: (1) Within-group PBSI comparisons showing CHR-P vs HC differences with t-statistics and p-values (PBSI-SA: t(2642)=-5.39, p<0.01; PBSI-CT: t(2788)=-9.11, p<0.01; PBSI-SV: t(2733)=-4.34, p<0.01); (2) Normative PBSI-Z scores identifying percentages deviating >1.5 SD (0.70% for SA, 7.47% for CT, 10.20% for SV). These metrics assess the degree of divergence from normative profiles rather than traditional model fit metrics. While not standard calibration metrics (like R² or RMSE), they do quantitatively assess the similarity/deviation of individual profiles relative to reference groups. The criterion of 'at least one quantitative metric assessing model fit or calibration' is partially met with these divergence metrics, though they serve a different purpose than traditional prediction accuracy measures.
nm9_model_performance_reference_cohort.supporting_text: There was greater within-group variability in all neuroanatomical profiles in the CHR-P group compared to the HC group based on significantly lower PBSI-SA (t(2642) = -5.39, p < 0.01), PBSI-CT (t(2788) = -9.11, p < 0.01), and PBSI-SV scores (t(2733) = -4.34, p < 0.01) | Of the 1579 CHR-P participants, 11 (0.70%) demonstrated marked deviation in PBSI-SA-Z scores, 118 (7.47%) in PBSI-CT-Z and 161 (10.20%) in PBSI-SV-Z | Of these participants, 17 demonstrated marked deviation in more than one phenotypic profile and just one participant in all three phenotypic profiles.

cr2_handling_of_clinical_covariates.reason: The criterion asks whether clinical covariates beyond basic demographics are considered in analyses. This is fully satisfied. The study investigated multiple clinical covariates as potential moderators of PBSI scores: (1) Medication status - both typical and atypical antipsychotic use examined; (2) Illness-related factors - transition status (CHR-T/CHR-NT), subgroup status (APS/BLIPS/GRD); (3) Symptom severity - baseline psychopathology using total CAARMS/SIPS severity z-scores (eMethods 3 describes conversion to z-scores to facilitate cross-instrument comparison). All multivariable regression models were adjusted for age and sex. The study explicitly tested associations between these clinical covariates and deviation scores (PBSI), finding no significant associations with transition, subgroup, or baseline psychopathology (all p>0.12), and only marginal association with typical antipsychotic use for PBSI-SV.
cr2_handling_of_clinical_covariates.supporting_text: In both PBSI analyses, we also investigated the potentially moderating effects of transition status (CHR-T/CHR-NT), subgroup status (APS/BLIPS/GRD), antipsychotic exposure, and overall baseline psychopathology (total CAARMS/SIPS severity z-scores, eMethods 3) on PBSI scores. All multivariable regression models were applied, adjusting for age and sex. | The Comprehensive Assessment of At-Risk Mental States (CAARMS) assessment and the Structured Interview for Prodromal Symptoms (SIPS) assessment represent different assessment and scoring procedures to reach classification of an at-risk mental state. Therefore, in order to facilitate the investigation of potential effects of psychopathology on PBSI scores across individuals at CHR-P, we converted the CAARMS summed psychosis severity score and SIPS summed psychosis severity score into z-scores, respectively. | There were no significant associations between PBSI scores and transition or subgroup status, baseline psychopathology (all p > 0.12), or current typical or atypical antipsychotic use on PBSI-SA or PBSI-CT scores. cr6_interpretation_of_deviation_scores.reason: All three criteria are fully satisfied: (1) The meaning and direction of deviation scores are explained - YES (higher PBSI scores [closer to 1] indicate greater similarity to reference group, lower scores indicate greater deviance; normative PBSI-Z scores represent degree of deviation from normative HC range); (2) Quantitative thresholds for defining categories are reported - YES (>1.5 SD threshold used to identify CHR-P individuals with marked deviation from normative profile, consistent with previous literature); (3) Clinical implications are discussed - YES (greater divergence in global neuroanatomical profiles in CHR-P vs HC across SA, CT, and SV; percentages deviating in each domain reported [0.70% SA, 7.47% CT, 10.20% SV]; importantly, no significant association with psychosis transition, suggesting heterogeneity exists irrespective of clinical outcomes; limitations discussed including that proportion with significantly deviant scores was low; potential utility for identifying subgroups for stratification purposes mentioned). The interpretation is thorough and clinically contextualized.
cr6_interpretation_of_deviation_scores.supporting_text: A higher PBSI score (closer to 1) indicates greater similarity in the neuroanatomical profile of an individual to other members of the same group, while a lower score indicates greater deviance in their neuroanatomical profile. | The resulting PBSI scores thus represent the degree of deviation from the 'normative' range and were transformed into z-scores (PBSI-CT-Z, PBSI-SA-Z, and PBSI-SV-Z). We set >1.5 SD as a threshold to identify individuals at CHR-P who most markedly deviated from the normative neuroanatomical profile, in line with previous work | Of the 1579 CHR-P participants, 11 (0.70%) demonstrated marked deviation in PBSI-SA-Z scores, 118 (7.47%) in PBSI-CT-Z and 161 (10.20%) in PBSI-SV-Z. Of these participants, 17 demonstrated marked deviation in more than one phenotypic profile and just one participant in all three phenotypic profiles. | There was greater within-group variability in all neuroanatomical profiles in the CHR-P group compared to the HC group based on significantly lower PBSI-SA (t(2642) = -5.39, p < 0.01), PBSI-CT (t(2788) = -9.11, p < 0.01), and PBSI-SV scores (t(2733) = -4.34, p < 0.01). PBSI-CT scores were substantially lower than PBSI-SA and PBSI-SV, signalling greater divergence specifically in CT profiles. | The within-diagnosis PBSI estimates revealed significantly lower scores across global SA, CT and SV amongst individuals at CHR-P, compared with HC. These findings signal greater divergence in neuroanatomical profiles within the CHR-P state across all three phenotypic measures. | There were no significant associations between PBSI scores and transition or subgroup status, baseline psychopathology (all p > 0.12) | Moreover, none of the variability metrics examined showed significant associations with a transition to psychosis. | Crucially, normative modelling of the PBSI also identified a subsample of CHR-P individuals who demonstrated marked deviation in reference to a 'normative' neuroanatomical profile. The identification of deviations from normative modelling is becoming increasingly popular in psychiatry and may aid in the classification of distinct subgroups. | To observe localised heterogeneity in these regions might signal discrepant neurobiological processes associated with psychosis-risk states (or with psychosis conversion in subsequent CHR-T/CHR-NT analyses), which may ultimately prove useful for stratification purposes in interventional research.
